1: The lightest element and the most abundant substance in the universe — three quarters of all ordinary matter.
Every water molecule in your body carries hydrogen forged in the first minutes after the Big Bang.
2: An inert noble gas so light it escapes Earth's gravity and leaks steadily into space.
Helium was found in the Sun's spectrum 27 years before anyone isolated it on Earth.
3: The lightest metal — soft enough to cut with a knife, and the heart of every rechargeable battery.
The lithium in your phone is older than the Earth. Most of it was made in the Big Bang.
4: A stiff, ultralight metal used in aerospace mirrors and X-ray windows. Highly toxic as dust.
The James Webb telescope's 18 mirror segments are beryllium — it barely flexes at −230 °C.
5: A metalloid that toughens glass. Borosilicate cookware and fiberglass both depend on it.
Boron is rare in the cosmos because stars destroy it. Cosmic rays shattering heavier atoms make most of it.
6: The backbone of every known living thing — and the same element in both graphite and diamond.
Carbon forms more compounds than all other elements combined: over ten million and counting.
7: Seventy-eight percent of the air you breathe, and locked into every protein and strand of DNA.
Pulling nitrogen out of the air to make fertilizer now feeds roughly half the people alive.
8: The element that made animal life possible, and nearly half the mass of Earth's crust.
Earth's oxygen is a waste product. Cyanobacteria dumped it into the air and caused a mass extinction.
9: The most reactive element there is. It attacks almost everything, including glass and water.
Fluorine is aggressive enough to burn asbestos — yet bonded into Teflon it becomes nearly inert.
10: A noble gas that glows a distinct orange-red when electrified. The original neon sign.
Every color other than orange-red in a 'neon' sign comes from a different gas or a coating.
11: A soft metal that fizzes violently in water. One half of ordinary table salt.
Your nerves fire by pumping sodium across cell membranes. Thought runs on this metal.
12: A light structural metal — and the single atom at the center of chlorophyll.
Every green leaf on Earth is green because of a magnesium atom catching sunlight.
13: The most abundant metal in the crust, yet it was once more precious than gold.
Aluminum was so hard to refine that Napoleon III served his most honored guests on aluminum plates.
14: The metalloid of sand, glass, and every microchip in the modern world.
A finished silicon wafer is purer than almost anything else humans make: 99.9999999% silicon.
15: Essential to DNA and ATP. One of its forms ignites on contact with air.
Phosphorus was first isolated from boiled-down urine, and it glows in the dark — hence 'light-bearer'.
16: A yellow nonmetal of volcanoes and vulcanized rubber, notorious for its smell.
Sulfur is one of the few elements the ancients found pure in the ground: the 'brimstone' of scripture.
17: A choking green gas that, bonded to sodium, becomes something you sprinkle on food.
Chlorinating drinking water may be the single largest life-saving intervention in public health history.
18: The third most common gas in the atmosphere, and a cheap inert shield for welding.
Argon fills the gap in double-glazed windows because it conducts heat worse than air does.
19: A reactive alkali metal that your nerves and muscles cannot work without.
Bananas are faintly radioactive: a fraction of all natural potassium is the isotope K-40.
20: The metal of bone, shell, and limestone. Fifth most abundant element in the crust.
The white cliffs of Dover are the compressed skeletons of trillions of microscopic algae.
21: A light, rare transition metal used in high-end bicycle frames and stadium lamps.
Mendeleev predicted scandium from a gap in his table years before anyone found it.
22: As strong as steel at half the weight, and unbothered by seawater or the human body.
Titanium is so biocompatible that bone will grow directly onto an implant and bond with it.
23: A hardening additive that makes tool steel tough. Also a promising flow-battery metal.
Its salts run through nearly every color of the rainbow depending on oxidation state.
24: The metal behind stainless steel's shine and its refusal to rust.
Chromium gives rubies their red and emeralds their green. Same atom, different crystal.
25: A hard, brittle metal that makes steel resistant to shattering under impact.
Manganese dioxide is the reason the alkaline battery in your drawer works at all.
26: The most-used metal on Earth, and the core of the planet itself.
Iron is where fusion stops paying. A star that reaches iron has minutes left before it collapses.
27: A magnetic metal of deep-blue pigments and lithium-ion cathodes.
Cobalt blue has colored Chinese porcelain and Egyptian glass for over two thousand years.
28: A corrosion-resistant metal found in coins, stainless steel, and battery chemistry.
Most 'nickels' are mostly copper. The coin is only a quarter nickel.
29: The first metal humans ever smelted, and still the default conductor of electricity.
The Statue of Liberty is copper, 2.4 mm thick — and green because it oxidized.
30: The sacrificial coating that stops steel from rusting, and an essential trace nutrient.
Galvanized steel survives by letting the zinc corrode instead. The coating dies for the metal.
31: A metal that melts in your hand, and the basis of LEDs and fast radio chips.
Gallium melts at 30 °C. A spoon made of it dissolves in a cup of tea.
32: The metalloid of the first transistors, now used in fiber optics and infrared lenses.
The first transistor, in 1947, was germanium. Silicon took over a decade later.
33: A metalloid infamous as a poison, now quietly essential to semiconductors.
Arsenic was the poison of choice for so long that it was nicknamed 'inheritance powder'.
34: A trace nutrient, and the photoconductor that made photocopying possible.
Early photocopiers coated a drum in selenium: it conducts electricity only where light hits it.
35: The only nonmetal that is liquid at room temperature. Heavy, fuming, red-brown.
Ancient Tyrian purple came from sea snails, and its color comes from bromine.
36: A noble gas used in high-performance lighting — and once in the definition of the meter.
From 1960 to 1983 the meter was officially defined by the wavelength of krypton-86 light.
37: A soft alkali metal so reactive it ignites in air. Used in atomic clocks.
Rubidium clocks are the workhorses that keep GPS satellites honest.
38: The metal that makes fireworks red — and a bone-seeker when radioactive.
Strontium-90 from 1950s bomb tests is still detectable in the teeth of people born then.
39: A rare-earth metal found in phosphors, lasers, and high-temperature superconductors.
The red phosphor in old color televisions was an yttrium compound.
40: A corrosion-proof metal that lines nuclear fuel rods and imitates diamond as cubic zirconia.
Zirconium is nearly transparent to neutrons, which is why reactor cores are built with it.
41: A superconducting metal used in MRI magnets and jet-engine alloys.
The magnet inside an MRI scanner is niobium wire, kept colder than deep space.
42: A high-melting metal that keeps steel strong at extreme temperature.
Some bacteria use molybdenum to crack nitrogen out of the air — nature's own fertilizer plant.
43: The lightest element with no stable isotope. Made in reactors, not mined.
Technetium was the first element ever created artificially. It now appears in 30 million medical scans a year.
44: A hard platinum-group metal used in electrical contacts and industrial catalysis.
A ruthenium tip is what makes a good fountain pen nib last a lifetime.
45: The catalytic metal in your car's exhaust, and often the most expensive of all.
Rhodium has traded at several times the price of gold. It is rarer than platinum.
46: A platinum-group metal that soaks up hydrogen like a sponge.
Palladium can absorb over 900 times its own volume in hydrogen gas.
47: The best electrical and thermal conductor of any element, and an ancient antimicrobial.
Photography ran on silver for 150 years. Every negative was silver grains turning dark.
48: A soft, toxic metal once everywhere in pigments and rechargeable batteries.
Cadmium yellow gave the Impressionists their brightest sunlight — and slowly poisoned the painters.
49: A soft metal whose oxide makes touchscreens both transparent and conductive.
Every phone screen you have ever tapped had a nearly invisible indium film reading your finger.
50: The metal that turned copper into bronze and started an age.
Cold turns tin into a crumbling gray powder. Church organ pipes have been destroyed by 'tin pest'.
51: A metalloid used in flame retardants and, historically, in cosmetics.
Egyptian kohl eyeliner was antimony sulfide — the same compound now used to stop fires spreading.
52: A scarce metalloid used in thin-film solar panels and thermoelectric generators.
Tellurium is rarer than platinum here yet common in the universe. Earth lost most of its share.
53: A dark violet halogen the thyroid cannot work without. A purple vapor when warmed.
Adding iodine to table salt eliminated an entire category of preventable brain damage.
54: A heavy noble gas used in brilliant arc lamps — and as a general anesthetic.
Xenon can put you under with almost no side effects. It is simply far too expensive to use.
55: The most reactive metal on the table. It explodes in water, and it defines the second.
One second is officially 9,192,631,770 oscillations of a cesium atom.
56: A dense alkaline-earth metal whose sulfate is the 'barium meal' of X-ray imaging.
Barium sulfate is safe to swallow only because it refuses to dissolve. The free ion is toxic.
57: The first lanthanide, used in camera lenses and nickel-metal-hydride batteries.
The battery pack in a first-generation Prius held about 10 kg of lanthanum.
58: The most abundant rare earth, used in catalytic converters and glass polish.
The spark in a cigarette lighter is cerium alloy shaving off and igniting in air.
59: A rare earth in powerful magnets, and in the yellow-green glass of welding goggles.
Welders' goggles are praseodymium-doped: it blocks the exact yellow glare of molten metal.
60: The metal behind the strongest permanent magnets ever made.
Your headphones, hard drive, and every EV motor use neodymium magnets. They hold a thousand times their own weight.
61: The only radioactive lanthanide with no stable isotope. Essentially absent from nature.
There is thought to be less than a kilogram of promethium in the entire Earth's crust.
62: A rare earth in heat-resistant magnets that keep working past 300 °C.
Samarium-cobalt magnets fly in spacecraft because they do not weaken when they get hot.
63: The rare earth behind the red and blue phosphors in screens and lighting.
Euro banknotes glow red under UV thanks to a europium compound — a forgery check built into the paper.
64: A rare earth used as an MRI contrast agent and as a neutron absorber.
Gadolinium injected before an MRI makes tumors light up by disturbing the water molecules around them.
65: A rare earth in green phosphors and in materials that change shape in a magnetic field.
Terbium alloys physically deform in a magnetic field — enough to turn a tabletop into a loudspeaker.
66: The additive that stops neodymium magnets from failing when they get hot.
Without a few percent dysprosium, an electric car's motor magnet would demagnetize itself.
67: The most magnetic element. Used in surgical lasers and magnet pole pieces.
Holmium has the highest magnetic moment of any element. It sits at the core of the strongest lab magnets.
68: The rare earth that makes long-haul fiber-optic internet possible.
Erbium amplifiers boost light directly, without converting it to electricity. The internet's quiet miracle.
69: The rarest stable lanthanide. Used in portable X-ray sources and lasers.
Thulium is so scarce that it was once priced by the milligram.
70: A rare earth at the heart of the most accurate clocks ever built.
An ytterbium lattice clock would drift less than one second over the age of the universe.
71: The last lanthanide. Dense, expensive, and used in PET scanner detectors.
Lutetium crystals turn gamma rays into flashes of visible light. They are the eyes of a PET scanner.
72: A refractory metal used in reactor control rods and in modern chip insulation.
Hafnium oxide replaced silicon dioxide inside transistors around 2007 and rescued Moore's law.
73: A dense, inert metal that forms the tiny capacitors inside every phone.
Tantalum is inert enough for surgical implants and dense enough to shape an explosive charge.
74: The highest melting point of any metal: 3,422 °C. The original lightbulb filament.
Tungsten carbide is hard enough to drill through rock and to cut other metals.
75: One of the rarest metals in the crust. Used in jet-engine turbine blades.
Rhenium has the second-highest melting point of all elements, and no ore of its own.
76: The densest naturally occurring element — twice the density of lead.
A liter of osmium weighs 22.6 kg. Its oxide, meanwhile, will blind you.
77: Nearly as dense as osmium, and the most corrosion-resistant metal known.
A worldwide iridium layer in the rock marks the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs.
78: A precious catalytic metal found in fuel cells, chemotherapy, and exhaust systems.
Cisplatin, a platinum drug, cures most testicular cancer. One of oncology's great successes.
79: The metal that never tarnishes. Humanity's store of value for six thousand years.
Every gold atom was forged in a neutron-star collision, then delivered here by asteroid impacts.
80: The only metal liquid at room temperature, and a potent neurotoxin.
Hat makers used mercury to felt fur, and it damaged their nerves — hence 'mad as a hatter'.
81: A soft, highly toxic metal once sold as rat poison, now used in infrared optics.
Thallium poisoning is nearly symptomless at first, which made it a favorite of poisoners.
82: Dense, soft, and toxic. The end point of most radioactive decay chains.
Roman plumbing was lead. The word 'plumber' comes from plumbum, its Latin name.
83: A brittle heavy metal, remarkably non-toxic, that grows spectacular rainbow crystals.
Bismuth is the heaviest practically non-toxic element. It is the active ingredient in Pepto-Bismol.
84: An intensely radioactive metalloid. A gram would glow and boil its own container.
Polonium-210 is roughly 250,000 times more toxic than hydrogen cyanide by weight.
85: The rarest naturally occurring element. Perhaps 25 grams exist in the whole crust.
Astatine has never been seen in bulk. A visible sample would vaporize from its own radioactivity.
86: A radioactive noble gas that seeps up out of rock and collects in basements.
Radon is the second leading cause of lung cancer after smoking — and it is invisible and odorless.
87: The second-rarest element, with a half-life measured in minutes.
No more than 30 grams of francium exist in the Earth's crust at any given moment.
88: A radioactive alkaline-earth metal that glows faintly blue in the dark.
Radium watch dials poisoned the women who painted them. The 'Radium Girls' won landmark labor rights.
89: The first actinide. Intensely radioactive, and glowing pale blue.
Actinium-225 is now used to deliver alpha particles directly into cancer cells.
90: A weakly radioactive metal, three times more abundant than uranium.
Thorium reactors are periodically hailed as the future of nuclear power, and periodically shelved.
91: A dense, scarce actinide with no application outside the research lab.
Protactinium is so troublesome to purify that only about 125 grams has ever been extracted.
92: The heaviest primordial element, and the fuel of both nuclear power and weapons.
Uranium glass fluoresces bright green under UV. Victorian households ate off mildly radioactive plates.
93: The first synthetic transuranic element, named for the planet past Uranus.
Neptunium was made in 1940 and named to continue the planetary sequence beyond uranium.
94: A synthetic metal that powers spacecraft and warheads alike.
Voyager 1 has run on plutonium-238 heat since 1977 and is now outside the solar system.
95: A synthetic actinide sitting inside millions of homes — in smoke detectors.
Your smoke alarm holds a speck of americium. Its radiation is what actually senses the smoke.
96: A synthetic actinide that glows in the dark from its own radioactivity.
Curium runs hot enough to serve as a power source, and it self-illuminates purple.
97: A synthetic element produced only in milligram quantities, ever.
Berkelium was the target used to synthesize tennessine. Element 117 exists because of it.
98: A synthetic neutron source used to start reactors and to prospect for gold.
A microgram of californium emits 170 million neutrons a minute. It costs about $27 million per gram.
99: Discovered in the fallout of the first hydrogen bomb test.
Einsteinium was found in debris from the 1952 Ivy Mike test, and kept classified for years.
100: The heaviest element that can be made in bulk by neutron bombardment.
Past fermium, elements must be built by smashing nuclei together one atom at a time.
101: A synthetic element made a single atom at a time in particle accelerators.
Mendelevium honors the man who left gaps in his table for elements nobody had found yet.
102: A synthetic actinide whose discovery was disputed for more than a decade.
Three separate labs claimed nobelium. The naming fight lasted far longer than the element does.
103: The last actinide, existing only for hours at a time inside a laboratory.
Lawrencium's electron configuration was measured only in 2015, and it breaks the expected pattern.
104: The first transactinide. A few atoms at a time, lasting seconds.
Rutherfordium sat at the center of a Cold War naming dispute between Berkeley and Dubna.
105: A synthetic superheavy element named for the Russian lab that helped find it.
Dubnium's name was the peace treaty that ended the 'Transfermium Wars'.
106: A superheavy element named after a living scientist — the first time that happened.
Seaborgium broke the convention against naming elements for the living, and started a rules fight.
107: A synthetic element with a half-life measured in seconds.
Only a few dozen atoms of bohrium have ever existed.
108: A superheavy element, probably a dense metal, known from a handful of atoms.
Hassium's chemistry has actually been studied — from about ten atoms, one at a time.
109: A synthetic element too short-lived for its properties to be measured directly.
Meitnerium honors Lise Meitner, who explained nuclear fission and was denied the Nobel for it.
110: A superheavy element whose longest-lived isotope survives about ten seconds.
Darmstadtium was made by firing nickel at lead for a week to produce a single atom.
111: A synthetic element predicted to be a noble, gold-like metal.
Roentgenium sits directly beneath gold, and is predicted to be even less reactive than it.
112: A superheavy element that may be a volatile liquid, like the mercury above it.
Copernicium might be a gas at room temperature — if anyone could collect enough to check.
113: The first element discovered by a Japanese research team.
Nihonium took RIKEN nine years of continuous bombardment to produce three atoms.
114: A superheavy element that appears to behave oddly like a noble gas.
Flerovium sits under lead but seems barely reactive. Relativity distorts its electrons that much.
115: A synthetic element that exists for fractions of a second.
Moscovium became briefly famous when a conspiracy theorist claimed UFOs were fueled by element 115.
116: A superheavy element named for the Livermore national laboratory.
Livermorium decays in about 60 milliseconds — barely time to confirm that it existed.
117: One of the newest elements, built from berkelium and calcium.
Tennessine needed a berkelium target so rare that only one lab on Earth could supply it.
118: The heaviest element ever made. The bottom-right corner of the table.
Oganesson should be a noble gas, but calculations suggest it is actually a reactive solid.
